## Summary
A defining feature of the [[fields|field]] \\( \mathbb{C} \\) is the absence of a total order compatible with its arithmetic operations. As established in the discussion of [[complex-numbers|complex numbers]], no relation \\( \leq \\) can be defined on \\( \mathbb{C} \\) so that it behaves consistently with addition and multiplication. Statements such as \\( z_1 < z_2 \\) are therefore meaningless for arbitrary complex numbers, and the comparison techniques available in \\( \mathbb{R} \\) do not transfer to the complex setting.

## Key Claims
- **Inequalities involving real and imaginary parts** — Let \\( z = a + bi \\) be a complex number, with \\( a = \mathrm{Re}(z) \\) and \\( b = \mathrm{Im}(z) \\).
- **Triangle inequality** — The most important inequality in the arithmetic of complex numbers is the triangle inequality, which asserts that the modulus of a sum is bounded by the sum of the moduli.
- **Reverse triangle inequality** — The triangle inequality has a companion result, often called the reverse triangle inequality, which provides a lower bound for the modulus of a difference.
- **Generalized triangle inequality** — The triangle inequality extends to finite sums of arbitrary length.
- **Cauchy-Schwarz inequality** — The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality is a quantitative refinement that relates sums of products of complex numbers to sums of their squared moduli.
- **Examples and applications** — A first illustration concerns the use of the elementary component inequalities.

nodes.markdown:
---
title: "Co-Evolving LLM Decision and Skill Bank Agents for Long-Horizon Tasks"
type: source
tags: [paper, llm-agents, reinforcement-learning, skills, games, co-evolution, umd]
date: 2026-04-22
source_file: raw/papers/2604.20987v1.md
arxiv_id: "2604.20987v1"
---

## Summary
Wu, Li, Shi et al. (Univ. of Maryland + USC + Good Start Labs + MBZUAI) introduce **COS-PLAY**, a multi-agent co-evolution framework for long-horizon game play. An LLM **decision agent** retrieves an active skill from a learnable **skill bank** and executes primitive actions conditioned on both intention and skill; an **agent-managed skill pipeline** segments unlabelled rollouts, learns compact skill contracts, and continually refines the bank. Both agents are trained with **GRPO**, closing the explore-learn-reuse loop without curated human demonstrations. On six game environments, an 8B-base-model COS-PLAY beats four frontier LLM baselines by **+25.1% average reward** on single-player games while remaining competitive on multi-player social-reasoning games.

## Key Claims
- **Co-evolution motivation.** The skill bank and decision agent are tightly coupled: a bank is only useful if the decider can select+execute its skills, and the decider is only as capable as its available skills. Existing work freezes one and improves the other; COS-PLAY trains both jointly.
- **Skills as a distinct abstraction layer.** Reusable, temporally extended behavior protocols extracted from trajectories — packaged with execution guidance and applicability *contracts*. Different from one-off tool calls or prompts.
- **Two questions framed.** (Q1) Should the bank and decision agent be learned jointly? (Q2) What properties make a bank useful for decisions? COS-PLAY is one of the first frameworks coupling LLM game decision-making with an agentic skill-bank pipeline for unsupervised discovery and continual refinement in a unified co-evolution loop.
- **Why games.** Long enough episodes for multi-skill chaining, recurring subgoals across episodes, cheap rollouts. Stress-test memory, planning, real-time action under delayed reward.
- **Empirical.** 8B base model + COS-PLAY beats four frontier LLM baselines by +25.1% average reward on single-player benchmarks; competitive on social-reasoning games.
- **Method components.** Decision agent maintains an intention and active skill; switches skills as needed. Skill-bank agent does unsupervised skill discovery + contract learning + bank curation. GRPO trains both: decision agent for retrieval+execution, skill-bank agent for segmentation+contracts+curation.

## Key Quotes
> "A skill bank is only useful if the decision agent can select and execute its skills effectively, and the decision agent is only as capable as the skills available to it."
> "We aim to learn a co-evolving skill bank directly from interaction."
> "One of the first frameworks to couple LLM-based game decision-making with an agentic skill-bank pipeline for unsupervised skill discovery and continual refinement in a unified co-evolution loop."

## Connections
- [[universityofmaryland|UniversityOfMaryland]] — primary affiliation.
- [[universityofsoutherncalifornia|UniversityOfSouthernCalifornia]] — co-affiliation.
- [[mbzuai|MBZUAI]] — Mohamed bin Zayed Univ. of AI co-affiliation.
- [[goodstartlabs|GoodStartLabs]] — co-affiliation.
- [[cosplay|COSPLAY]] — proposed framework.
- [[skillbank|SkillBank]] — central abstraction.
- [[grpo|GRPO]] — RL algorithm for both agents.
- [[longhorizontasks|LongHorizonTasks]] — task domain.
- [[balrog|BALROG]] / [[vsbench|VSBench]] / [[videogamebench|VideoGameBench]] / [[visgym|VisGym]] — long-horizon game benchmarks cited.
- [[voyager|Voyager]] — predecessor skill-library system.
- [[polyskill|PolySkill]] / [[sage|SAGE]] / [[skillrl|SkillRL]] / [[scalar|SCALAR]] / [[xskill|XSkill]] — sibling skill-augmented RL systems.
- [[memweaver|Memweaver]] / [[procmem|ProcMEM]] / [[cascade|CASCADE]] / [[uimem|UIMem]] / [[memrl|MemRL]] / [[memskill|MemSkill]] — memory-augmented agents cited.
- [[2604.27707-agentic-memory-is-a-memo]] — directly relevant: that paper argues only weight consolidation crosses the generalization gap; COS-PLAY's skill-bank agent updates *both* an external bank *and* the LLM weights via GRPO, partially addressing the memo critique.
- [[2605.02396-heavyskill]] — internalized parallel-reason vs. externalized skill bank as alternate loci for "skill".
- [[2604.24026-ssl-skill-representation]] — provides a candidate structured representation for the contracts COS-PLAY's skill-bank agent learns.

## Contradictions
- Treats games as the right testbed for co-evolution, in tension with productivity-grounded synthetic environments ([[2604.28181-synthetic-computers-at-scale]]) and benchmark-replication framings ([[2604.25067-frontier-coding-agents-c4]]). Aligned with [[2604.21590-agenticqwen]]'s data-flywheel intuition (continually generated harder data) but with skills rather than tasks as the unit.

nodes.markdown:
---
title: "ODS Ch.13: Data Structures for Integers"
type: source
tags: [book, data-structures, tries, integers]
date: 2026-05-10
source_file: raw/ods-python.pdf
book: "Open Data Structures (in pseudocode)"
author: "Pat Morin"
chapter: 13
pages: "257-274"
---

## Summary
SSet implementations specialized to w-bit integer keys. Three structures of strictly increasing sophistication. **BinaryTrie** stores n integers as root-to-leaf paths in a binary tree of depth w; leaves are doubly-linked into a sorted list, with auxiliary `jump` pointers to handle missing children — gives O(w) add/remove/find. **XFastTrie** speeds up find from O(w) to O(log w) by hashing the trie's nodes by prefix and binary-searching levels — but at the cost of O(n·w) space. **YFastTrie** restores O(n) space and O(log w) for add/remove by storing only one-in-w "representatives" in an XFastTrie and partitioning the rest into Treap-style buckets.

## Key Claims
- **BinaryTrie**: each integer x ∈ {0,...,2^w−1} is a root-to-leaf path; leaves are linked into a sorted doubly-linked list. find/add/remove all O(w). Space O(n·w) in the worst case.
- **The jump pointer trick**: each interior node u with a missing child stores a pointer u.jump to the smallest leaf in its (would-be) subtree larger than x (or symmetrically the largest smaller). This lets find(x) cut off at the first missing branch and jump straight to the linked-list neighbour.
- **XFastTrie**: store the set of trie *prefixes at each level* in a hash table. find(x) does binary search over the w levels (log w hash lookups), each finding the deepest existing prefix of x; jump pointer then completes the search.
- **YFastTrie**: SSet built by storing every w-th element (a "representative") in an XFastTrie and bucketing the remaining elements between representatives in a treap or skiplist of size O(w). find(x) → O(log w); add/remove → O(log w) expected, since updates rebalance buckets and only sometimes promote/demote a representative.
- **All three SSets beat the O(log n) bound** of comparison-based balanced BSTs whenever w = o(log² n).

## Key Quotes
> "The BinaryTrie performs all three SSet operations in O(w) time. This is not very impressive, since any subset of {0,...,2^w − 1} has size n ≤ 2^w, so that log n ≤ w."
> "The XFastTrie speeds up the search in a BinaryTrie by using hashing. With this speedup, the find(x) operation runs in O(log w) time."

## Connections
- [[ods-06-binary-trees]] — BinaryTrie is a binary tree over key bits.
- [[ods-03-linked-lists]] — leaves of the trie form a doubly-linked sorted list.
- [[ods-05-hash-tables]] — XFastTrie hashes prefixes per level.
- [[ods-07-random-binary-search-trees]] — YFastTrie's bucket structure can be a treap.
- [[ods-11-sorting-algorithms]] — radix-sort exploits the same per-bit indexing as the trie.
- [[modulo-operator]] — bit-extraction via shift and mod.

## Contradictions
- The XFastTrie's O(n·w) space is impractical for large w; YFastTrie restores O(n) but adds implementation complexity. The chapter frames this trie family as primarily a theoretical contribution — a constructive proof that integer SSet operations can beat the comparison-tree lower bound.

## Summary
Given a positive integer \\(n\\), a root of unity of order \\(n\\) is a [[complex-numbers|complex number]]  \\(z\\) satisfying the [[equations|equation]] \\[ z^n = 1 \\]

type: source

## Summary
Singh et al. (Microsoft Research + NUS) argue that interpretability tools used by Agentic Data Science (ADS) systems were designed for humans, not agents. They introduce **AGENTIC-IMODELS**, an autoresearch loop in which a coding agent (e.g. Claude Code) iteratively modifies a scikit-learn-compatible Python class to optimize jointly for predictive performance and a novel **LLM-based simulatability** interpretability metric — measuring whether an LLM can answer questions about a fitted model by reading only its `__str__`. Discovered models extend the Pareto frontier on held-out datasets and new tests, and improve four downstream ADS agents by **8–73%** on the BLADE benchmark.

## Key Claims
- **Interpretability mismatch** — existing tools (decision trees, GAMs, rule lists, plus visualizations) were designed for humans, often impeding agents.
- **LLM-graded simulatability** — replaces human experiments; tests probe predictions, feature effects, counterfactuals from `__str__` alone.
- **Autoresearch loop** — coding agent proposes Python-class modifications; loop scores both metrics across 65 tabular datasets; rank-averaging avoids RMSE-noise sensitivity.
- **Pareto improvement** — evolved AGENTIC-IMODELS dominate baselines (TabPFN, EBM, GBM, PyGAM, OLS, Ridge, FIGS, HSTree, MLP) jointly on accuracy and agent-interpretability.
- **Generalization** — improvements transfer to held-out datasets and unseen interpretability tests.
- **Downstream wins** — 8–73% gain on BLADE for Copilot CLI, Claude Code, Codex when equipped with evolved models vs standard interpretability tools.
- **Qualitative novelty** — evolved models combine known algorithms in new ways and present themselves in agent-amenable forms.

## Key Quotes
> "Rather than designing data-science tools to be interpretable by humans, we aim to design tools that are interpretable by agents."
> "Equipping four different ADS agents with the evolved models improves their performance on the BLADE end-to-end benchmark by 8%–73%."

## Connections

- [[NationalUniversityOfSingapore]] — co-affiliation.

- [[imlbook-interpretability]] — canonical Molnar treatment of the property the paper redefines for agents.
- [[imlbook-tree]] — decision trees explicitly cited as a baseline interpretable family.

- [[imlbook-extend-lm]] — generalized additive models (GAMs) explicitly cited as a baseline.
- [[imlbook-shap]] — Shapley-additive interpretability standard the simulatability metric ultimately competes against.

## Contradictions
- Reframes interpretability away from human-centered evaluation; partially in tension with literature that equates interpretability with sparsity/decision-tree depth — those metrics may not align with agent-graded simulatability.

Foundational treatment of sets: definitions (enumeration vs set-builder), cardinality, subsets, power sets, partitions, set operations (union, intersection, complement, difference, symmetric difference), De Morgan's laws, Cartesian products, and the set-theoretic definition of the ordered pair.

## Key Claims
- A set is a collection of distinguishable objects (elements); membership is unambiguous.
- Cardinality of a power set: \\(|\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^n\\) for finite \\(A\\) with \\(n\\) elements.
- Inclusion-exclusion: \\(|A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|\\).
- A partition of \\(A\\) is a family of non-empty, pairwise disjoint subsets covering \\(A\\); it corresponds bijectively to an equivalence relation.
- De Morgan's laws: \\((A \cup B)^c = A^c \cap B^c\\) and \\((A \cap B)^c = A^c \cup B^c\\); they generalise to arbitrary finite collections.
- Symmetric difference + intersection give the powerset of a set the structure of a Boolean ring.
- The Kuratowski definition of the ordered pair: \\((a, b) = \{\{a\}, \{a, b\}\}\\) — yields \\((a,b)=(c,d) \iff a=c \land b=d\\).

## Key Quotes
> "A set can be described by enumeration or by the set-builder notation."
> "Two sets are equal if and only if each is contained in the other."

- [[real-numbers|RealNumbers]] — Cartesian plane as \\(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\\).
- [[rings|Rings]] — symmetric difference + intersection give a Boolean ring structure.
- [[BooleanAlgebra]] — set operation identities are the foundation of Boolean algebra.
- [[PropositionalLogic]] — De Morgan's laws correspond to logical equivalences \\(\neg(P\lor Q) \equiv \neg P \land \neg Q\\).

## Summary
Given an angle \\( \theta \\) in standard position on the [[unit-circle|unit circle]], the acute angle formed between its terminal side and the horizontal axis is called the reference angle of \\( \theta \\), and is usually denoted by \\( \alpha \\). The reference angle provides a direct link between the trigonometric functions of a generic angle and those of an acute angle in the first quadrant, where all values are positive and computable from elementary geometric considerations.

- **Reduction formulas for \\( \pi/2 - \alpha \\)** — Consider now an angle of the form \\(\frac{\pi}{2}-\alpha\\) where \\( \alpha \\) denotes an acute angle in the first quadrant.
- **Reduction formulas for \\( \pi + \alpha \\)** — Consider now an angle of the form \\(\pi+\alpha)\\), where \\( \alpha \\) denotes an acute angle.
- **Reduction formulas for \\( \pi - \alpha \\)** — Consider now an angle of the form \\(\pi-\alpha\\) where \\( \alpha \\) denotes an acute angle.
- **Reduction formulas for \\( 3\pi/2 + \alpha \\)** — Consider now an angle of the form \\(\frac{3\pi}{2}+\alpha\\) where \\( \alpha \\) denotes an acute angle.
- **Reduction formulas for \\( 3\pi/2 - \alpha \\)** — Consider now an angle of the form \\(\frac{3\pi}{2}-\alpha\\) where \\( \alpha \\) denotes an acute angle.
- **Reduction formulas for \\( 2\pi - \alpha = -\alpha \\)** — Consider finally an angle of the form \\(2\pi-\alpha\\) where \\( \alpha \\) denotes an acute angle.

type: source

## Summary
The skiplist is a beautiful randomized data structure that gives O(log n) expected time for all List and SSet operations through a stack of geometrically-thinning singly-linked lists. Heights are determined by independent coin tosses: an element appears in L_r with probability 2^(−r). Two applications: **SkiplistSSet** (sorted set with expected O(log n) find/add/remove) and **SkiplistList** (random-access list with expected O(log n) get/set/add/remove). Lemma 4.1: the expected length of any search path is at most 2·log n + O(1).

## Key Claims
- **Construction by geometric sampling.** L_0 holds all n elements; element x is included in L_r if r consecutive coin tosses come up heads. Expected height of any node is 1; expected total space is O(n).
- **Search-path bound.** Lemma 4.1: the expected length of the search path from sentinel to any node is at most 2·log n + O(1). Proof postponed to §4.4.
- **SkiplistSSet** implements SSet operations in O(log n) expected time. Search descends right-then-down: at each level, advance while u.next[r].x < x; otherwise drop to level r−1.
- **SkiplistList** uses the same skeleton but stores element *count* in each next-pointer instead of values; supports get(i)/set(i)/add(i,x)/remove(i) in O(log n) expected.
- **Coin tosses simulated with `pick_height()`**: pick a random 32-bit integer z and return the count of trailing 1 bits — equivalent to flipping coins until tails.
- **No rebalancing**, no rotations: simplicity is the headline feature. The randomness in *node heights* (not in input order) is what bounds search-path length.

## Key Quotes
> "The efficiency of skiplists relies on their use of randomization."
> "The expected length of the search path for any node, u, in L_0 is at most 2 log n + O(1) = O(log n)."

## Connections
- [[ods-03-linked-lists]] — base layer of the skiplist is exactly an SLList.
- [[ods-07-random-binary-search-trees]] — sibling randomized SSet via random insertion order.
- [[ods-09-red-black-trees]] — deterministic alternative with worst-case O(log n).
- [[ods-01-introduction]] — interfaces (SSet) defined here; randomization analysis tools introduced here.
- [[probability]] / [[binomial-coefficient]] — coin-toss expectation analysis.

## Contradictions
None.

nodes.label: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
nodes.markdown:
---
title: "BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding"
type: source
tags: [paper, transformer, pretraining, language-model, bidirectional, foundational]
date: 2018-10-11
sources: []
source_file: raw/1810.04805v2.pdf
last_updated: 2026-05-10
---

## Summary
Devlin, Chang, Lee & Toutanova ([[Google]] AI Language) introduce **BERT** — Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers — a pre-trained Transformer encoder that conditions on left **and** right context at every layer. Two unsupervised pre-training objectives — a **Masked Language Model** (MLM, after the Cloze task of Taylor 1953) and **Next Sentence Prediction** (NSP) — replace the unidirectional next-token objective used by ELMo and OpenAI GPT, enabling a single pre-trained model to be fine-tuned with just one extra output layer for diverse downstream tasks. BERT advances the state of the art on 11 NLP benchmarks, including GLUE (80.5, +7.7 points absolute), MultiNLI (86.7, +4.6), SQuAD v1.1 F1 (93.2, +1.5) and SQuAD v2.0 F1 (83.1, +5.1). Together with [[1706.03762-attention-is-all-you-need]] it is the second load-bearing paper underlying every modern LLM.

## Key Claims
- **Deep bidirectionality is the major lever.** Ablations isolate bidirectional pre-training from training data, scheme and hyperparameters; "LTR & No NSP" (a GPT-style left-to-right baseline trained on BERT's data and scheme) is strictly worse on every GLUE/SQuAD task. Adding a randomly-initialized BiLSTM on top of an LTR model recovers some of the gap on SQuAD but hurts GLUE — bidirectionality must be in the pre-trained representations, not bolted on at fine-tune time.
- **Masked LM beats left-to-right LM.** Standard conditional LMs can only train left-to-right or right-to-left because bidirectional conditioning would let each token "see itself" in a multi-layer context. Randomly masking 15% of WordPiece tokens (80% `[MASK]` / 10% random / 10% unchanged, to mitigate the pre-train/fine-tune mismatch where `[MASK]` never appears) lets a deep bidirectional Transformer be pre-trained. MLM converges marginally slower than LTR but begins outperforming "almost immediately".
- **Next Sentence Prediction helps QA and NLI.** Binarized task — given sentence A, is B the actual next sentence or a random one — yields 97–98% accuracy and gives meaningful gains on QNLI / MNLI / SQuAD (≥0.5–1.5 F1 each).
- **One unified architecture across tasks.** Apart from output layers, the same architecture is used for sentence-pair classification, single-sentence classification, span prediction (SQuAD) and sequence tagging (CoNLL NER). All parameters are fine-tuned end-to-end with a task-specific output head, plus the `[CLS]` token's final hidden state used as the aggregate sequence representation.
- **Fine-tuning beats feature-based use for most tasks, but feature-based is competitive.** On CoNLL-2003 NER, concatenating the last four hidden layers as fixed features and feeding them to a BiLSTM is only 0.3 F1 behind full fine-tuning — useful when downstream tasks need non-Transformer architectures or pre-computed embeddings.
- **Model size matters even for tiny downstream tasks.** Scaling from BERT_BASE (L=12, H=768, A=12, 110M params) to BERT_LARGE (L=24, H=1024, A=16, 340M params) yields strict accuracy improvements on all four GLUE tasks studied, including MRPC (3.6k examples) — the first convincing demonstration that extreme model size also helps very small downstream tasks, provided the model has been sufficiently pre-trained.
- **Architecture-level near-identity with GPT.** BERT_BASE was chosen to match OpenAI GPT's parameter count; the substantive differences are (1) bidirectional vs left-only self-attention, (2) BooksCorpus + Wikipedia vs BooksCorpus alone, (3) `[SEP]` / `[CLS]` / segment embeddings learned during pre-training, (4) larger batch (128k vs 32k tokens), (5) task-specific fine-tuning learning rate. Ablations attribute the majority of the gain to (1) plus the two pre-training tasks.

## Key Quotes
> "BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers."

> "Standard conditional language models can only be trained left-to-right or right-to-left, since bidirectional conditioning would allow each word to indirectly 'see itself,' and the model could trivially predict the target word in a multi-layered context."

> "Unfortunately, standard conditional language models can only be trained left-to-right or right-to-left… To train a deep bidirectional representation, we simply mask some percentage of the input tokens at random, and then predict those masked tokens."

> "We believe that this is the first work to demonstrate convincingly that scaling to extreme model sizes also leads to large improvements on very small scale tasks, provided that the model has been sufficiently pre-trained."

## Architecture Reference (constants)
- **BERT_BASE**: L=12 Transformer encoder layers, H=768 hidden, A=12 heads, FFN=4H=3072, 110M params.
- **BERT_LARGE**: L=24, H=1024, A=16, FFN=4096, 340M params.
- **Tokenizer**: [[WordPiece]] with 30,000 vocab; `[CLS]` prepended, `[SEP]` separates segments; learned segment-A/segment-B embeddings; learned positional embeddings (max 512).
- **Pre-training corpus**: BooksCorpus (800M words) + English Wikipedia (2,500M words, text-only). Critical to use document-level not shuffled-sentence corpus to learn long contiguous sequences.
- **Pre-training schedule**: batch 256 × 512 = 128k tokens/batch, 1,000,000 steps (≈40 epochs over 3.3B words). Adam (lr=1e-4, β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, L2=0.01, warmup 10k, linear decay), dropout 0.1, GELU activation. 90% of steps at seq-len 128 then 10% at 512 to learn positional embeddings.
- **Hardware**: BERT_BASE — 4 Cloud TPUs (16 chips), 4 days; BERT_LARGE — 16 Cloud TPUs (64 chips), 4 days.
- **Fine-tune ranges**: batch ∈ {16, 32}, LR (Adam) ∈ {5e-5, 4e-5, 3e-5, 2e-5}, epochs ∈ {2, 3, 4}; dropout fixed at 0.1.

## Results Reference (headline)
- **GLUE Test (avg)**: BERT_LARGE 82.1, BERT_BASE 79.6, OpenAI GPT 75.1, prior SOTA 74.0.
- **MultiNLI (m/mm)**: BERT_LARGE 86.7/85.9 vs prior 82.1/81.4.
- **SQuAD v1.1 Test EM/F1**: single-model 85.1/91.8, ensemble + TriviaQA 87.4/93.2.
- **SQuAD v2.0 Test EM/F1**: 80.0/83.1 (+5.1 F1 over prior best).
- **SWAG Test**: 86.3 (+27.1 over ESIM+ELMo, +8.3 over GPT; human-expert baseline 85.0).
- **CoNLL-2003 NER Test F1**: 92.8 fine-tuned, 92.4 feature-based (last 4 layers concat to BiLSTM).

## Connections
- [[1706.03762-attention-is-all-you-need]] — supplies the Transformer encoder BERT stacks; BERT is the first paper to demonstrate that the encoder half alone, pre-trained at scale, transfers to virtually every NLU task.
- [[Google]] — author affiliation (Google AI Language); same company that produced the Transformer paper.
- [[Transformer]] — the underlying architecture; BERT is "a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder".
- [[Pretraining]] — BERT is the canonical demonstration that *unsupervised* pre-training on large text corpora followed by *supervised* fine-tuning is the dominant transfer-learning recipe for NLP.
- [[MaskedLanguageModel]] — the central pre-training objective introduced (or popularized) here.
- [[NextSentencePrediction]] — the auxiliary pre-training objective for sentence-pair tasks.
- [[WordPiece]] — the subword tokenization scheme used (30k vocab).
- [[chainofthought]] — emerges in decoder-style LLMs that built on this pretraining-then-finetuning recipe.
- All 2026 LLM-agent papers in this wiki implicitly inherit the pretrain-then-finetune paradigm BERT established, even when their finetuning step is replaced by RL ([[grpo]], [[rlvr]]).

## Contradictions
None. This paper predates every 2026 source in the LLM corpus by ~8 years and supplies (with [[1706.03762-attention-is-all-you-need]]) the architectural and training-recipe substrate they all build on.

## Notes
- v1 posted 11 Oct 2018; v2 (this file) is the 24 May 2019 NAACL camera-ready, including ablations originally only in v1's appendix.
- Code and pre-trained checkpoints at https://github.com/google-research/bert.
- Cited inspiration for MLM: Wilson Taylor's 1953 *Cloze procedure* — the same gap-filling task psycholinguists used to measure readability.
- Architecture decisions deliberately matched OpenAI GPT to permit clean controlled comparison. The contrast with GPT (and with ELMo's shallow L-R + R-L concatenation) is the paper's central pedagogical move (Figure 3).

## Summary
Foundational treatment of binary trees: a connected, undirected, finite graph with no cycles where no vertex has degree > 3. Most computer-science applications use **rooted, ordered** binary trees (left vs. right child). The chapter establishes vocabulary (depth, height, ancestor, descendant, subtree, leaf, external nodes) and presents **BinarySearchTree**, an unbalanced binary search tree implementing SSet operations in time proportional to the height of the tree (worst-case O(n) for skewed trees). Covers recursive vs. iterative traversal, including how to traverse without recursion using the parent pointer (avoids stack overflow on tall trees).

## Key Claims
- **Tree terminology.** Depth(u) is the path length from u to root. Height(u) is the longest path from u to any descendant. Height(tree) = height(root). External nodes (n+1 of them in a tree with n real nodes) are useful as algorithmic conveniences.
- **Recursive vs iterative traversal.** Recursion is concise but stack-bounded by tree height. The non-recursive `traverse2()` uses the parent pointer plus a "previous" pointer to compute the next move from any node.
- **BinarySearchTree** stores keys with the BST invariant: all keys in left subtree < u.x < all keys in right subtree. find(x) walks down comparing; insert places new leaf at the search-failure point; remove with two children uses successor-replacement.
- **Performance** is O(height). With adversarial inputs, height can be Θ(n), motivating the balanced trees in [[ods-07-random-binary-search-trees]], [[ods-08-scapegoat-trees]], [[ods-09-red-black-trees]].
- **Breadth-first traversal** uses a Queue; depth-first uses a Stack (or recursion).
- **Size and height computed recursively** in O(n) by recursive descent.

## Key Quotes
> "Mathematically, a binary tree is a connected, undirected, finite graph with no cycles, and no vertex of degree greater than three."
> "Using recursion this way produces very short, simple code, but it can also be problematic. The maximum depth of the recursion is given by the maximum depth of a node in the binary tree."

## Connections

- [[ods-10-heaps]] — implicit binary tree stored in an array (Eytzinger's method).
- [[ods-12-graphs]] — BFS / DFS algorithms generalized.
- [[ods-13-data-structures-for-integers]] — BinaryTrie is a binary tree over bits of integers.

- **Transpose** — The transpose of a matrix \\( A \\) of dimensions \\( m \\times n \\), denoted \\( A^{\\mathrm{T}} \\), is the matrix of dimensions \\( n \\times m \\) obtained by interchanging the rows and columns of \\( A \\).

## Summary
Individual Conditional Expectation (ICE) plots display one line per instance that shows how the instance's prediction changes when a feature changes. An ICE plot [@goldstein2015peeking] visualizes the dependence of the prediction on a feature for *each* instance separately, resulting in one line per instance of a dataset. The values for a line (and one instance) can be computed by keeping all other features the same, creating variants of this instance by replacing the feature's value with values from a grid, and making predictions with the black box model for these newly created instances.…

## Key Claims
- **Examples** — @fig-ice-bike shows ICE plots for the [bike rental prediction](#bike-data).
- **Centered ICE plot** — There's a problem with ICE plots: Sometimes it can be hard to tell whether the ICE curves differ between data points because they start at different predictions.
- **Derivative ICE plot** — Another way to make it visually easier to spot heterogeneity is to look at the individual derivatives of the prediction function with respect to a feature.
- **Strengths** — Individual conditional expectation curves are **intuitive to understand**.
- **Limitations** — ICE curves **can only display one feature** meaningfully, because two features would require the drawing of several overlaying surfaces, and you would not see anything in the plot.
- **Software and alternatives** — ICE plots are implemented in the R packages `iml` [@molnar2018iml] (used for these examples), `ICEbox`, and `pdp`.

type: source

## Summary
Two hash-table implementations of the USet interface, plus a treatment of hash-code design. **ChainedHashTable** uses an array of linked lists (collision resolution by chaining), maintaining the load-factor invariant n ≤ length(t). **LinearHashTable** uses open addressing with linear probing. Both achieve O(1) expected time per operation provided the hash function is sufficiently random. The chapter introduces **multiplicative hashing** as the workhorse function — `hash(x) = ((z·x) mod 2^w) div 2^(w−d)` with z random odd in {1,...,2^w−1} — and proves Pr{hash(x) = hash(y)} ≤ 2/2^d for any x ≠ y. Closes with the engineering question of computing hash *codes* for compound objects, arrays, and strings.

## Key Claims
- **ChainedHashTable invariant**: n ≤ length(t) keeps expected list length ≤ 1. Resize doubles or halves the table on the same factor-3 hysteresis as [[ods-02-array-based-lists]].
- **Expected list length lemma (5.2)**: for any x, E[length of t[hash(x)]] ≤ n_x + 2 where n_x is the number of occurrences of x. So find(x), remove(x) both run in O(1) expected.
- **Multiplicative hashing** with a random odd integer z gives a 2-universal-style guarantee Pr{hash(x) = hash(y)} ≤ 2/2^d (Lemma 5.1). The proof goes through Lemma 5.3, a number-theoretic uniqueness fact about z·q mod 2^w on odd q.
- **LinearHashTable** stores values directly in the array and uses linear probing on collision; analysis (§5.2.1) bounds expected probe length given a tabulation-hashing-style function (§5.2.3).
- **Hash codes for primitives**: integers hash to themselves; floats reinterpret bits. **For strings/arrays**: treat as a polynomial in a random base z modulo a prime p — this gives an O(k)-time hash with provable collision bounds (§5.3.3).
- **Tabulation hashing** (§5.2.3) gives an alternative with strong theoretical guarantees: precompute a table of random values, XOR by byte position.

## Key Quotes
> "The performance of a hash table depends critically on the choice of the hash function."
> "Pr{hash(x) = hash(y)} ≤ 2/2^d ."

## Connections
- [[ods-01-introduction]] — defines USet; argues to prefer it over SSet when ordering is unneeded.
- [[ods-02-array-based-lists]] — same amortized doubling/halving argument is reused.
- [[ods-03-linked-lists]] — bucket containers in ChainedHashTable.
- [[ods-12-graphs]] — uses hash tables to implement adjacency-set graph operations in O(1) expected.
- [[modulo-operator]] — multiplicative hashing relies on `mod 2^w` arithmetic.

## Summary
Two graph representations and the two foundational traversal algorithms. **AdjacencyMatrix**: an n×n boolean matrix a[i][j] = (i,j) ∈ E. add_edge / remove_edge / has_edge in O(1); in_edges / out_edges in O(n); space O(n²). Suited to dense graphs. **AdjacencyLists**: an array of lists, one per vertex; add_edge in O(1); has_edge / remove_edge in O(deg); in/out_edges in O(deg). Space O(n+m). Then **breadth-first search** (BFS) using a Queue — visits vertices in non-decreasing order of distance from a source — and **depth-first search** (DFS) using a Stack or recursion. Both run in O(n+m) on adjacency lists, O(n²) on adjacency matrices.

## Key Claims
- **AdjacencyMatrix theorem (12.1)**: edge ops O(1), in/out_edges O(n), space O(n²) bits.
- **Bonus**: matrix-multiplication a² counts paths of length 2; iterating gives all-pairs shortest paths in O(log n) matrix multiplications — connects to algebraic graph algorithms.
- **AdjacencyLists** typically preferred for sparse graphs (m = o(n²)). Lists implemented as ArrayStacks for O(1)-index access; DLLists give O(deg) remove_edge.
- **BFS**: starting at r, mark r visited and enqueue. Repeatedly dequeue u, enqueue every unvisited neighbour. Visits in distance order; computes shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
- **DFS**: visit u, mark visited, recurse on unvisited neighbours (or use explicit stack). Yields a DFS forest with edges classified as tree/back/forward/cross.
- **Both run in O(n + m)** on adjacency-list representation; O(n²) on adjacency-matrix.

## Key Quotes

nodes.markdown:
---
title: "Skills as Verifiable Artifacts: A Trust Schema and a Biconditional Correctness Criterion for Human-in-the-Loop Agent Runtimes"
type: source
tags: [paper, ai-safety, llm-agents, security, hitl, supply-chain, skills]
date: 2026-05-01
source_file: raw/papers/2605.00424v1.md
arxiv_id: "2605.00424v1"
---

## Summary
Alfredo Metere (Metere Consulting) argues a SKILL.md package is **untrusted code until verified**. Signature + clearance is not behavioral verification; the runtime must default to HITL for irreversible calls and only relax that gate as a function of an explicit, immutable per-skill verification level. The paper specifies a trust schema (manifest tuple with classification label, capability set, signer, version, verification level), a four-state HITL lifecycle for irreversible side-effects, and a **biconditional correctness criterion** — every observed corpus delta must match an approved-and-executed audit record and vice versa — which doubles as a benchmark a candidate skill-verification procedure must pass on an adversarial ensemble. Ten normative guidelines (G1–G10) abstracted from the reference implementation **enclawed** sketch a portable runtime profile for any SKILL.md-adopting harness.

## Key Claims
- **Skills are a new supply-chain surface.** A skill is a persistent prompt-injection vector that survives context truncation; the analogous attack class (memory/KB poisoning) has already been demonstrated in the wild.
- **Default-untrusted is the only stable HITL discipline.** Without verification, HITL must fire on every irreversible call, which degrades into rubber-stamping at scale; the fix is verification, not weaker gates.
- **Verification happens at bootstrap, never at runtime.** Verification levels (`unverified` / `declared` / `tested` / `formal`) are pinned to the signed manifest pre-bootstrap and are immutable for the session — a fixed enum, not a continuous trust score, to prevent the agent from arguing itself into permission gradients.
- **No agent mutation of loaded skills.** Any attempted modification is itself an irreversible capability that walks the HITL gate and is hash-chained-audited; on approval it produces a new artifact requiring re-verification.
- **Capability vocabulary is finite and irreversibility-tagged.** `net.egress`, `fs.read`, `fs.write.rev`, `fs.write.irrev`, `tool.invoke`, `spawn.proc`, `publish`, `pay`, `mutate.schema`. The reversible/irreversible split is the design's load-bearing distinction.
- **Biconditional correctness criterion.** `delta(s0, s1) == { approved-and-executed records }` (multiset, projected on op-and-target). Catches gate bypass (F1), audit forgery (F2), approved-but-failed-silently (F3), wrong-target execution (F4). Does not catch read-only exfiltration, TOCTOU races, or attacker-coincident actions.
- **Adversarial-ensemble evaluation.** K agents biased toward destruction (cleaner / consolidator / auditor / critic) over R rounds on a SHA-256-baselined corpus; verdict is mechanical (binary, deterministic for fixed broker policy).
- **Ten guidelines G1–G10.** Capability bootstrap, deny-by-default, mandatory classification, clearance-bounded signing, hash-chained audit, reversible/irreversible split, biconditional post-hoc check, adversarial test corpus, named configuration profiles (strict vs dev — no feature-flag continuum), and a no-bypass-switch invariant.

## Key Quotes
> "A skill is untrusted code until it is verified, and the runtime that loads it must enforce that default rather than infer trust from a signature, a clearance, or a registry of origin."
> "The skill is the instruction; the model is the executor."
> "Verification is what buys the runtime permission to stop asking, and only for what the verification covered."

## Connections
- [[metereconsulting|MetereConsulting]] — institutional author.
- [[enclawed|Enclawed]] — open-source reference implementation.
- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]] — artifact format being verified.
- [[humanintheloop|HumanInTheLoop]] — HITL gate and lifecycle.
- [[biconditionalcorrectness|BiconditionalCorrectness]] — central criterion.
- [[capabilitygate|CapabilityGate]] — runtime layer between LLM and external world.
- [[trustroot|TrustRoot]] — append-only signer set with one-shot lock.
- [[belllapadula|BellLaPadula]] — classification lattice borrowed from MAC.
- [[verificationlevels|VerificationLevels]] — unverified/declared/tested/formal enum.
- [[hashchainedaudit|HashChainedAudit]] — gate-event log primitive.
- [[adversarialensemble|AdversarialEnsemble]] — evaluation shape.
- [[promptinjection|PromptInjection]] — primary threat vector.
- [[supplychainsecurity|SupplyChainSecurity]] — analogous to package-manager attack history.
- [[claudecode|ClaudeCode]] — major SKILL.md harness.

## Contradictions
- Stands in tension with current harness practice (cited as collapsing signature + clearance into trust). Complementary to but distinct from [[2605.03310-coordination-architectural-layer|Nechepurenko & Shuvalov]]: both call for separating concerns previously fused inside agent harnesses (coordination there, verification here), but on orthogonal axes. Tightens the contract for the agent skills increasingly produced by [[2605.03808-agentic-imodels|AGENTIC-IMODELS]]-style autoresearch loops, where self-generated skills are an explicit threat actor in this paper's threat model.

## Summary
Two ways to use randomization to keep an unbalanced BinarySearchTree balanced in expectation. **Random Binary Search Tree**: insert n distinct keys in a uniformly random permutation order. Lemma 7.1 shows the expected search-path length is H_(x+1) + H_(n−x) − O(1) = 2·ln n + O(1), via the indicator-random-variable trick on harmonic numbers. **Treap**: assign each key a uniformly random priority and maintain heap order on priorities (smallest priority at the root) plus BST order on keys via tree rotations during add/remove. The Treap dynamically simulates a random binary search tree without controlling the input order.

## Key Claims
- **The fundamental observation**: in a BST built from random permutation π, key i is on the search path for x ∈ {0, ..., n−1} iff i appears before any of {i+1, ..., ⌊x⌋} in π. This makes the path-length expectation a sum of harmonic-derived probabilities.
- **Lemma 7.1**: expected search path length is H_(x+1) + H_(n−x) − O(1), bounded by 2·ln n + O(1) = O(log n).
- **Harmonic number bounds**: ln k < H_k ≤ ln k + 1 (provable via integral comparison ∫_1^k (1/x)dx = ln k).
- **Treap**: random priorities make the resulting tree distributed identically to a random BST, regardless of insertion order. add(x) is BST insert + bubble-up by rotations to restore heap order; remove(x) is rotate-to-leaf + delete.
- **Both structures give O(log n) expected time** for find/add/remove. The randomness is over the choice of priorities (treap) or insertion permutation (RBST), not over the input.

## Key Quotes
> "If we choose a random permutation of 0,...,14 and add its elements, one by one, into a BinarySearchTree, then we are more likely to get a very balanced tree than we are to get a very unbalanced tree."
> "The expected length of the search path for x is H_(x+1) + H_(n−x) − O(1)."

## Summary
Pointer-based implementations of the List interface. The trade-off vs. array-based: get(i)/set(i) become O(1+min{i,n−i}) instead of O(1), but adding or removing at any *referenced* node is O(1). Three structures: **SLList** (singly-linked, supports Stack and FIFO Queue in O(1)), **DLList** (doubly-linked with a sentinel **dummy** node, supports Deque in O(1)), and **SEList** (Space-Efficient: a doubly-linked list whose nodes are small ArrayDeques of size ≤ b+1, getting nearly array-like space efficiency while keeping pointer-style modifiability).

## Key Claims
- **Linked-list trade-off.** Lose O(1) random access; gain O(1) splice/insert/remove given a node reference. Holds for *any* position in the list.
- **SLList implements Stack + FIFO Queue in O(1)/op** by maintaining `head` and `tail` pointers plus `n`. Push/pop on head; FIFO add/remove use tail/head respectively.
- **DLList Deque trick**: a single **dummy sentinel** node turns every list into a non-empty cycle, eliminating null-checks on head and tail and reducing the special-case count substantially.
- **DLList random access is O(1+min{i, n−i})** by walking from the closer end via dummy.next or dummy.prev.
- **SEList** stores blocks of an ArrayDeque inside each linked-list node; with block size √n it gives O(1) wasted space per node and amortized O(1+min{i,n−i}/b) for random-access ops. Adding/removing only locally rebalances neighbouring blocks via spread/gather operations.
- **Amortized analysis of spread/gather** (§3.3.5) parallels the array-doubling argument from [[ods-02-array-based-lists]].

## Key Quotes
> "The primary disadvantage is that we lose the ability to access any element using get(i) or set(i,x) in constant time."
> "Perhaps the cleanest way to take care of all these special cases in a DLList is to introduce a dummy node."

## Connections
- [[ods-02-array-based-lists]] — primary alternative implementation of the List interface.
- [[ods-01-introduction]] — defines List, Stack, Queue, Deque interfaces.
- [[ods-04-skiplists]] — augments singly-linked lists with extra pointers for O(log n) random access.
- [[ods-05-hash-tables]] — ChainedHashTable uses linked lists as bucket containers.
- [[ods-13-data-structures-for-integers]] — BinaryTrie threads its leaves into a doubly-linked list.

## Contradictions

## Summary
Lyu, Wang et al. (Alibaba) train **AgenticQwen** — a family of 8B / 30B Qwen-based agentic models — primarily on synthetic data via multi-round RL using two complementary **data flywheels**. The **reasoning flywheel** rewrites model errors into harder verifiable variants (self-instruct expansion + persona injection + multi-teacher consensus filter). The **agentic flywheel** expands linear single-path workflows into multi-branch behavior trees, with simulated users intentionally pushing the model into unexpected branches to force decision-making. On public benchmarks AgenticQwen 8B/30B competes with much larger open-source models; on Alibaba's internal industrial agent system it closes the gap with Qwen3-235B on search/data-analysis tasks at significantly lower serving cost.

## Key Claims
- **Industrial gap.** Frontier proprietary models (GPT-5, Claude) are too expensive at million-user scale; major foundation-model developers rarely release small models with strong agentic capabilities, leaving a deployment gap.
- **Two-stage RL.** Reasoning RL: GRPO-style training on Omni / 2WikiMultiHopQA / HotpotQA with binary final-answer reward + web-search and code-interpreter tools. Agentic RL: rubric-based 0–1 rewards over verifiable subgoals with simulated users + tools (Qwen3-235B as simulator).
- **Reasoning data flywheel.** Self-instruct expansion (change values, add constraints, deepen theory), persona-injection rewrites (physics / chemistry scenarios), consensus filter (multi-teacher agreement check) — keep only items where independent teachers agree.
- **Agentic data flywheel.** Round-by-round expansion: linear → branched workflows. Branches injected by simulated users introducing unexpected conditions (sold-out tickets → search HSR / nearby airport, gold-tier compensation logic, etc.). Back-translates branched workflows into new training contexts.
- **Diversity over volume.** Synthetic samples saturate quickly when homogeneous; the flywheels exist precisely to keep diversity growing as the model improves.

nodes.markdown:
---
title: "Agentic Harness Engineering: Observability-Driven Automatic Evolution of Coding-Agent Harnesses"
type: source
tags: [paper, llm-agents, coding-agents, harness, evolution, observability, fudan, peking-university]
date: 2026-04-30
source_file: raw/papers/2604.25850v3.md
arxiv_id: "2604.25850v3"
---

## Summary
Lin, Liu, Pan et al. (Fudan + Peking U + Shanghai Qiji Zhifeng) introduce **Agentic Harness Engineering (AHE)** — a closed-loop framework that automates the previously manual craft of coding-agent harness design. AHE rests on three matched **observability pillars**: ❶ **component observability** exposes seven editable harness component types as files at fixed mount points; ❷ **experience observability** distills millions of raw trajectory tokens into a layered drill-down evidence corpus; ❸ **decision observability** pairs every edit with a self-declared prediction verified against the next round's task-level outcomes. Ten iterations lift Terminal-Bench 2 pass@1 from **69.7% → 77.0%**, beating human-designed Codex CLI (71.9%) and self-evolving baselines ACE (68.9%) and TF-GRPO (72.3%). The frozen harness transfers cross-benchmark (SWE-bench-verified at 12% fewer tokens) and cross-base-model (+5.1 to +10.1 pp on three alternate model families).

## Key Claims
- **Harness, not just model.** Long-horizon coding-agent performance is materially shifted by harness design even with the base model held fixed; optimal harnesses are model-specific and must be re-adapted as base models change.
- **Bottleneck is observability, not optimizer capability.** Once the evolution agent receives structured context over a clear action space, it converges reliably on better harness designs.
- **Seven editable component types.** System prompt, tool description, tool implementation, middleware, skill, sub-agent configuration, long-term memory — each at a fixed mount point in the **NexAU** framework, loosely coupled so component-level edits don't cascade.
- **Falsifiable-contract evolution.** A change manifest pairs each edit with a prediction; if the next round disconfirms the prediction at task-level outcome, the edit is reverted at file granularity. Prevents the loop from collapsing into trial-and-error.
- **Empirical gains.** Terminal-Bench 2 pass@1 69.7 → 77.0% over 10 iterations. SWE-bench-verified: best aggregate success at 12% fewer tokens than the seed without re-evolution. Cross-family +5.1 to +10.1 pp gains on three alternate base-model families — largest where the base model is furthest from saturation.
- **Where the gains live (ablation).** Tools, middleware, and long-term memory each carry the improvement on their own; the system prompt alone regresses. **Factual harness structure transfers; prose-level strategy does not.**
- **Two limits acknowledged.** Components interact non-additively, capping aggregate gain when stacking edits; self-attribution is reliable for fixes but blind to regressions — regression foresight is named as the clearest open problem.

## Key Quotes
> "Harness engineering remains a manual craft, because automating it faces a heterogeneous action space across editable components, voluminous trajectories that bury actionable signal, and edits whose effect is hard to attribute."
> "Once the evolution agent receives structured context over a clear action space, it can reliably converge on better harness designs."
> "Factual harness structure transfers across tasks and models whereas prose-level strategy does not."

Specifically, every non-empty subset of \\( \mathbb{R} \\) that is bounded above possesses a least upper bound that remains within \\( \mathbb{R} \\). ## Summary
A [[complex-numbers|complex number]] \\( z \\) is an expression of the form \\( z = a + bi \\), where \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) are [[properties-of-real-numbers|real numbers]] and \\( i \\) is the imaginary unit, characterized by the defining relation \\( i^2 = -1 \\).

## Key Claims
- **Sum and difference of complex numbers** — The sum and difference of two complex numbers are defined componentwise, by operating separately on the real and imaginary parts.
- **Product of complex numbers** — The product of two complex numbers is defined by applying the distributive property and the fundamental relation \\( i^2 = -1 \\).
- **Properties of the complex conjugate** — The complex [[complex-numbers|conjugate]] satisfies several algebraic identities that follow directly from its definition.
- **Division of complex numbers** — To divide two complex numbers, we multiply both the numerator and the denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator.
- **Reciprocal of a complex number** — The reciprocal of a nonzero complex number \\( z = a + bi \\) is the multiplicative inverse \\( z^{-1} \\), defined by the condition \\( z \cdot z^{-1} = 1 \\).
- **Multiplication and division in trigonometric form** — The operations of multiplication and division acquire a particularly transparent geometric interpretation when complex numbers are expressed in trigonometric or exponential form.

title: "Self-Improving Pretraining: using post-trained models to pretrain better models"
type: source
tags: [paper, llm, pretraining, reinforcement-learning, llm-as-judge, fair, meta]
date: 2026-04-05
source_file: raw/papers/2601.21343v3.md
arxiv_id: "2601.21343v3"

## Summary
FAIR at Meta proposes **Self-Improving Pretraining**: replace next-token prediction with prefix-conditioned suffix generation trained by RL, using an existing strong post-trained model as both **rewriter** (producing better suffixes) and **judge** (scoring rollouts) so safety, factuality and quality are baked in early instead of patched after the fact. They also introduce **thinking mid-training**, an intermediate stage that augments pretraining data with interleaved reasoning traces optimized via SFT + RL with a judge.

## Key Claims
- **Pretrain stage is the right place for safety/factuality** — patterns acquired in pretraining largely dictate downstream behavior; layered post-training cannot fully overwrite them.
- **Sequence-level objective replaces next-token** — policy generates a length-N suffix from the prefix; rewards come from a judge comparing rollouts to the original suffix and to a rewritten suffix.
- **Two roles for the teacher** — rewriter (improves suffix quality / safety, augments diversity), judge (per-axis scoring of rollouts/suffix/rewrite).
- **Empirical gains** — 36.2% relative factuality improvement, 18.5% safety, up to 86.3% win rate on overall quality vs standard continual pretraining; 31.1% absolute quality win-rate gain from-scratch.
- **Thinking mid-training** — interleaving reasoning traces during the mid-train stage improves reasoning benchmarks via SFT+RL with a judge.

## Key Quotes
> "Many desirable behaviors such as safety, factuality, overall generation quality, and reasoning ability are only added at a late stage, even though the patterns learned earlier strongly shape a model's capabilities."
> "Leveraging stronger models to shape pretraining data and objectives is a promising direction for building more capable and reliable language models."

## Summary
An interval is a subset of the real line with the property that, whenever two points belong to it, every point lying between them also belongs to it. More precisely, a subset \\( I \subseteq \mathbb{R} \\) is an interval if and only if, for every pair of points \\( a, b \in I \\) with \\( a < b \\), the entire set \\( \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a \leq x \leq b\} \\) is contained in \\( I \\). This property, known as convexity on the [[real-numbers|real line]], distinguishes intervals from arbitrary subsets of \\( \mathbb{R} \\) such as finite sets or unions of disconnected pieces.

## Key Claims
- **Bounded intervals** — A bounded interval is one that is contained within a finite portion of the real line, that is, one for which there exist real numbers \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) with \\( a \leq b \\) such that the interval is a subset of \\( [a, b] \\).
- **Unbounded intervals** — An unbounded interval extends indefinitely in at least one direction.
- **Operations on intervals** — Given two intervals, one may form new sets by combining them through the standard set-theoretic operations of intersection and union.
- **Intervals and neighborhoods** — A concept closely related to intervals and central to mathematical analysis is that of a neighborhood of a point.
- **Length of an interval** — The length of a bounded interval with endpoints \\( a \\) and \\( b \\) is defined as \\( b - a \\), regardless of whether the endpoints are included or excluded.
- **Characterization of intervals** — A subset of the real line is said to be connected if it cannot be written as the union of two disjoint non-empty open sets.

title: "Synthetic Computers at Scale for Long-Horizon Productivity Simulation"
type: source

---

## Summary
Ge, Peng, Cheng & Gao (Microsoft) introduce **Synthetic Computers at Scale**: a persona-driven methodology that elaborates a persona → user profile → planned filesystem → populated directory hierarchy with content-rich artifacts (docs, spreadsheets, presentations). Conditioned on each synthetic computer, a **setup agent** creates user-specific objectives requiring ~one month of human work, and a **work agent** acts as that user across the computer for >8 hours runtime / >2,000 turns per simulation. They release 100 synthetic computers (50 Windows-style + 50 macOS-style) and retrospective reports for 500 simulations from a 1,000-computer preliminary run.

## Key Claims
- **Productivity work is context-heavy.** Realistic deliverables are grounded in existing files, history, prior decisions, and evolving project state — not isolated tasks.
- **Synthesize the context, not just the task.** Without realistic environments to condition on, synthetic data degenerates into toy workflows. The methodology fills the user-environment gap that real-trajectory collection cannot scale through (privacy, cost).
- **Three-stage computer creation.** Persona → detailed user profile (identity, occupation, organization, responsibilities, recent work history) → planned filesystem (artifacts, folder organization, naming conventions, inter-artifact relationships) → instantiated populated computer.
- **Two-agent simulation loop.** Setup agent generates objectives requiring multiple professional deliverables (reports, spreadsheets, presentations) ≈ one month of human work; work agent navigates filesystem for grounding, coordinates with simulated collaborators, iteratively revises deliverables until objectives complete.
- **Scale claim.** Personas are abundant at billion scale (Ge et al., 2024); the pipeline can in principle scale to millions or billions of synthetic computers with compute. Per-simulation cost: 8 h runtime, 2,000+ turns.
- **Empirical validation.** Long-horizon trajectories produce both process signals (search/plan/revise/coordinate/recover) and outcome signals (deliverable quality); fine-tuning on these yields significant in-domain and out-of-domain agent performance gains.
- **Positioning.** Argued as a foundational substrate for **agent self-improvement** and **agentic RL** in long-horizon productivity scenarios — explicit complement to coding-agent grounding (Cursor, Claude Cowork).

## Key Quotes
> "Productivity work is context-heavy by nature."
> "Synthetic data must synthesize the context, not only the task."
> "Each simulation corresponds to about a month of work for the computer's user, requires over 8 hours of agent runtime, and spans more than 2,000 turns on average."

## Connections

- [[microsoftresearch|MicrosoftResearch]] — research umbrella.

- [[cursor|Cursor]] — repository-grounded predecessor.

## Contradictions
- Implicit tension with [[2604.27707-agentic-memory-is-a-memo|Xu, Dai & Zhang]]: this paper's premise that long-horizon trajectories yield "rich experiential learning signals" assumes those signals can be turned into capability — which the memory paper says only holds when consolidation reaches the weights, not the context. The two papers are complementary if simulations feed weight-level fine-tuning (which they do here) and contradictory if interpreted as accumulating retrieval traces.

## Summary
Sakana AI introduces the **Conductor**, a 7B reasoning model trained end-to-end with reinforcement learning to design multi-agent workflows for stronger worker LLMs. The Conductor outputs three Python lists per task — natural-language subtasks, worker IDs, and per-step access lists — letting it freely shape topologies (BoN, sequential chains, trees) plus targeted prompt engineering. With randomized agent pools and a recursive option that lets the Conductor select itself, the model attains state-of-the-art on LiveCodeBench and GPQA Diamond while outperforming costlier multi-agent baselines.

## Key Claims
- **End-to-end RL coordination** — language-model coordination strategies emerge from reward maximization without explicit prompt-engineering supervision; uses GRPO with a two-tier (format / correctness) reward.
- **7B beats heavyweights via orchestration** — a 7B Conductor surpasses any individual worker on its training dataset and beats prior multi-agent methods at lower call cost.
- **Workflow representation** — each step is a `(subtask string, worker id, access list)` tuple; output structure is parsed from a single chain-of-thought response (Figure 2).
- **Adaptability to arbitrary worker pools** — finetuning with randomized agents at each step generalizes to open- and closed-source workers, removing dependence on a fixed agent set.
- **Recursive topologies as a new TTS axis** — allowing the Conductor to address itself unlocks online iterative adaptation as a tunable inference-time scaling dimension.

## Key Quotes
> "A 7B Conductor attains state-of-the-art results on challenging reasoning benchmarks such as LiveCodeBench and GPQA Diamond."
> "Common strategies such as prompt engineering, refinement, and even meta-prompt optimization, naturally emerge from end-to-end reward maximization."

title: "ODS Ch.11: Sorting Algorithms"
type: source

author: "Pat Morin"
chapter: 11

## Summary
Two parts. **Comparison-based sorting**: merge-sort, quicksort, heap-sort — three asymptotically-optimal Θ(n log n) algorithms whose lower bound is matched by the information-theoretic comparison-tree argument (Theorem at §11.1.4: any comparison sort makes Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case). **Non-comparison sorting**: counting sort and radix sort use array indexing on integer keys to break the n log n barrier — counting sort is O(n + U) for keys in {0, ..., U−1}; radix sort applied k times sorts integers in {0, ..., n^c − 1} in O(c·n) time.

## Key Claims
- **Merge-sort** runs in Θ(n log n) by divide-and-conquer recurrence. Theorem 11.1: at most n log n comparisons. Proof goes through the recursion tree (Figure 11.2).
- **Quicksort** uses a random pivot for expected Θ(n log n) — analysis via the same harmonic-number argument as [[ods-07-random-binary-search-trees]] (the recursion tree is *exactly* a random binary search tree built from input).
- **Heap-sort** = build BinaryHeap in O(n) + extract-min n times — Θ(n log n), in-place when reusing the input array.
- **Lower bound** on comparison-based sorting (§11.1.4): the decision tree for any comparison sort has n! leaves; minimum height = log(n!) = Θ(n log n) by Stirling. So no comparison sort beats Θ(n log n).
- **Counting sort**: for keys in {0,...,U−1}, count occurrences in O(n+U), then write keys back in sorted order. Linear when U = O(n).
- **Radix sort**: apply counting sort k times, once per digit, from least to most significant. For integer keys in {0,...,n^c − 1} with base n, total time is O(c·n).

## Key Quotes
> "If we allow other operations besides comparisons, then all bets are off. Indeed, by using array indexing, it is possible to sort a set of n integers in the range {0,...,n^c − 1} in O(cn) time."
> "No algorithm that uses only comparisons can avoid doing roughly n log n comparisons in the worst case and even the average case."

## Connections
- [[ods-07-random-binary-search-trees]] — quicksort recursion tree is a random BST.
- [[ods-10-heaps]] — heap-sort uses BinaryHeap.
- [[ods-06-binary-trees]] — comparison-tree lower-bound argument.
- [[ods-13-data-structures-for-integers]] — radix-sort intuition extends to BinaryTrie indexing.
- [[factorial]] / [[logarithms]] — Stirling's approximation grounds the n log n lower bound.

## Contradictions
None.

nodes.markdown:
---
title: "Attention Is All You Need"
type: source
tags: [paper, transformer, attention, machine-translation, foundational]
date: 2017-06-12
sources: []
source_file: raw/1706.03762v7.pdf
last_updated: 2026-05-10
---

## Summary
Vaswani et al. (Google Brain + Google Research + University of Toronto) propose the **Transformer**, a sequence transduction architecture built entirely on attention — eliminating recurrence and convolution. By replacing the recurrent encoder/decoder of prior NMT systems with stacked **multi-head self-attention** plus position-wise feed-forward layers, the model becomes massively parallelizable, reduces the path length between any two positions to O(1), and trains in a fraction of the time. The Transformer (big) sets new state-of-the-art BLEU scores on WMT 2014 (28.4 EN-DE, 41.8 EN-FR) at ~1/4 the training cost of the prior best, and generalizes to English constituency parsing. This paper is the architectural foundation of every subsequent large language model.

## Key Claims
- **Recurrence is eliminable.** A model based "solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely" can outperform the best recurrent and convolutional sequence transduction models on machine translation while training significantly faster.
- **Self-attention has constant maximum path length.** A self-attention layer connects all positions with O(1) sequential operations, vs. O(n) for recurrent layers and O(log_k n) for ByteNet-style dilated convolutions — making long-range dependencies easier to learn.
- **Scaled dot-product attention.** `Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)·V`. The 1/√d_k scaling counteracts the variance growth of dot products at large d_k that would otherwise push softmax into low-gradient regions.
- **Multi-head attention beats single-head.** With h=8 heads of dimension d_k=d_v=64, the model jointly attends to information from different representation subspaces; "averaging inhibits this" with a single head. Ablation row (A) shows both too few and too many heads hurt BLEU.
- **Three uses of attention in the Transformer.** (1) Encoder-decoder attention — decoder queries attend over encoder outputs. (2) Encoder self-attention — each position attends to all positions in the previous layer. (3) Decoder self-attention — masked to forbid attending to future positions, preserving auto-regressive property.
- **Sinusoidal positional encoding.** With no recurrence/convolution, position is injected via additive sine/cosine encodings of geometrically progressing wavelengths (2π → 10000·2π). Learned positional embeddings perform "nearly identical"; sinusoidal version is preferred because it may extrapolate to lengths unseen in training.
- **Translation results.** Transformer (big): 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 EN-DE (>2.0 BLEU above prior best, including ensembles); 41.8 BLEU on WMT 2014 EN-FR (single-model SOTA, ~1/4 the training FLOPs of the previous best). Trained 3.5 days on 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs.
- **Generalization to parsing.** A 4-layer Transformer reaches 91.3 F1 (WSJ-only) and 92.7 F1 (semi-supervised) on Penn Treebank constituency parsing, beating most prior task-specific models without task-specific tuning.
- **Interpretable heads.** Attention visualizations (appendix) show individual heads tracking long-range dependencies, performing anaphora resolution, and exhibiting structures aligned with syntax.

## Key Quotes
> "We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely."

> "Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this."

> "We suspect that for large values of d_k, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients. To counteract this effect, we scale the dot products by 1/√d_k."

> "We are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks. We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video."

## Architecture Reference (constants)
- Base model: N=6 encoder/decoder layers, d_model=512, d_ff=2048, h=8 heads, d_k=d_v=64, P_drop=0.1, ε_ls=0.1, ~65M params.
- Big model: N=6, d_model=1024, d_ff=4096, h=16, P_drop=0.3, ~213M params.
- Optimizer: Adam (β₁=0.9, β₂=0.98, ε=10⁻⁹), inverse-sqrt LR schedule with warmup_steps=4000.
- Training: WMT 2014 EN-DE (~4.5M sentence pairs, 37K BPE shared vocab); EN-FR (36M pairs, 32K word-piece vocab); ~25K source/target tokens per batch.

## Connections
- [[Transformer]] — the architecture introduced here; the load-bearing concept page.
- [[SelfAttention]] — the core mechanism (queries, keys, values from the same sequence).
- [[MultiHeadAttention]] — h parallel attention heads concatenated and projected.
- [[ScaledDotProductAttention]] — the specific attention function with 1/√d_k scaling.
- [[PositionalEncoding]] — sinusoidal injection of position information.
- [[EncoderDecoder]] — the high-level structure inherited from prior seq2seq work.
- [[1409.3215-seq2seq]] — the direct architectural predecessor; same encoder-decoder framing, recurrent [[LSTM]] backbone replaced here by [[SelfAttention]].
- [[Google]] — primary author affiliation (Google Brain + Google Research).
- [[chainofthought]] — downstream LLM behavior pattern enabled by Transformer scale.
- [[grpo]] — RL backbone applied to Transformer-based LLMs in the 2026 papers.
- All foundational LLM papers in this wiki ([[2512.04388-conductor]], [[2601.21343-self-improving-pretraining]], [[2604.21590-agenticqwen]], [[2605.02396-heavyskill]], [[2605.02572-long-horizon-llm-training]], etc.) presuppose the Transformer as base architecture.

## Contradictions
None with current wiki content. This paper *predates* every other source in the LLM corpus by ~9 years and supplies the architectural substrate they all build on.

## Notes
- Code released at https://github.com/tensorflow/tensor2tensor.
- 31st NeurIPS (NIPS 2017), Long Beach, CA.
- v7 of arXiv:1706.03762 (2 Aug 2023) — minor corrections to the original 2017 paper; equations and headline results unchanged.
- All eight authors are listed as equal contributors; ordering is randomized.

type: source

## Summary
Red-black trees are simulated 2-4 trees: BSTs in which each node is colored red or black, with two invariants — every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes (**black-height**), and no two red nodes are adjacent (**no-red-edge**). Together these force height ≤ 2·log n, give worst-case O(log n) add/remove, and bound the amortized number of rotations per update at constant. RBTs are the workhorse SSet in production library code (Java Collections Framework, parts of the C++ STL, Linux kernel). The chapter develops them via 2-4 trees first (cleaner intuition), then maps to left-leaning red-black trees (each red node leans left; corresponds to a 2-, 3-, or 4-node).

## Key Claims
- **Three properties making red-black trees popular** (over skiplists, treaps, scapegoat trees):
  1. height ≤ 2 log n;
  2. add/remove run in O(log n) **worst-case** time;
  3. amortized rotations per add/remove is O(1) — the time to *find* x dominates the time to update around it.
- **2-4 tree primer**: every internal node has 2, 3, or 4 children; all leaves at the same depth. Height ≤ log n. add(leaf) splits overflowing nodes upward; remove(leaf) merges/redistributes underflowing nodes upward.
- **Red-black mapping**: each 2-node = black; 3-node = black with one red child; 4-node = black with two red children. Black-height equals 2-4-tree height.
- **Cost of niceness**: implementation is the most complex of the SSets in this book — careful case analysis for rotations and recolorings during add and remove is required (the bug surface is large).

## Key Quotes
> "Red-black trees are one of the most widely used data structures. They appear as the primary search structure in many library implementations."
> "Maintaining a bound of 2 log n on the height is not easy. It requires a careful analysis of a number of cases. We must ensure that the implementation does exactly the right thing in each case."

## Connections
- [[ods-06-binary-trees]] — base BinarySearchTree, extended with color invariants.
- [[ods-07-random-binary-search-trees]] / [[ods-08-scapegoat-trees]] — alternative balancing strategies (randomized / amortized).
- [[ods-04-skiplists]] — sibling SSet with simpler implementation but only expected guarantees.
- [[ods-14-external-memory-searching]] — B-trees are 2-4 trees generalized to disk-block degree.
- [[ods-01-introduction]] — defines SSet interface red-black trees implement.

## Contradictions
- Strictly better than skiplists/treaps/scapegoat trees on worst-case bounds — but the implementation is significantly more complex. The book frames this as a deliberate engineering trade-off.

## Summary
Logistic regression models the probabilities for classification problems with two possible outcomes. It's an extension of the linear regression model for class outcomes.[^actually-probabilities]

## Key Claims
- **Don't use linear regression for classification** — The linear regression model can work well for regression, but fails for classification.
- **Theory** — A solution for classification is logistic regression.
- **Interpretation** — The interpretation of the weights in logistic regression differs from the interpretation of the weights in linear regression since the outcome in logistic regression is a value between 0 and 1.
- **Logistic regression is multiplicative** — On the level of probabilities, logistic regression is not linear in the features.
- **Enhance interpretation with model-agnostic methods** — If you want to interpret the outcome on the level of probabilities, then you have to use model-agnostic methods, such as the [partial dependence plot](#pdp).
- **Example** — We use logistic regression to predict [whether a penguin is female](#penguins) for Chinstrap penguins based on body measurements.
- **Strengths** — Many of the pros and cons of the [linear regression model](#limo) also apply to the logistic regression model.
- **Limitations** — Logistic regression has been widely used by many different people, but it struggles with its restrictive expressiveness (e.g., interactions must be added manually), and other models may have better predictive performance.
- **Software** — I used the `glm` function in R for all examples.

## Summary
A group is one of the most fundamental structures in abstract algebra. The concept arises when one isolates the essential properties shared by many mathematical objects: the [[natural-numbers|integers]] under addition, the nonzero [[real-numbers|real numbers]] under multiplication, the symmetries of a geometric figure, and the invertible [[matrices|matrices]] of a given size all exhibit the same abstract pattern. In formal terms, a group is a set \\(G\\) together with a binary operation \\(\cdot : G \times G \to G\\) satisfying the following four axioms:

## Key Claims
- **Properties** — Several consequences follow from the previous axioms.
- **Algebraic hierarchy** — Groups are the most elementary objects in the hierarchy of algebraic structures.
- **Order of an element** — The order of an element \\(a\\) in a group \\(G\\) is the smallest positive integer \\(n\\) such that \\(a^n = e\\), where \\(e\\) is the identity element and the notation \\(a^n\\) denotes the product of \\(a\\) with itself \\(n\\) times.
- **Examples** — The set \\(\mathbb{Z}\\) equipped with ordinary addition forms an abelian group.
- **When the axioms fail** — A good way to appreciate the group axioms is to look at pairs consisting of a set and an operation that almost form a group, but fail on one specific point.
- **Cyclic groups** — A group \\(G\\) is called cyclic if there exists an element \\(g \in G\\) such that every element of \\(G\\) can be written as a power of \\(g\\), that is:
- **Subgroups** — A subset \\(H\\) of a group \\(G\\) is called a subgroup if \\(H\\) is itself a group under the operation inherited from \\(G\\).
- **Group homomorphisms and isomorphisms** — A group homomorphism is a [[Functions|function]] between two groups that preserves the group structure.
