## Summary
Liang, Wang, Liang & Liu (Peking University) argue that the dominant SKILL.md text-heavy format collapses semantically distinct properties — invocation interface, execution phases, action / resource-use evidence — into one natural-language surface, creating a representational bottleneck for skill discovery and risk assessment. They introduce **SSL (Scheduling-Structural-Logical)**, the first explicit three-layer typed JSON representation for agent skill artifacts, grounded analogically in Schank & Abelson's classical cognitive-linguistic theories. An LLM-based **normalizer** converts existing SKILL.md files into SSL. Empirically, SSL beats text-only baselines on Skill Discovery (MRR@50 **0.649 → 0.729**) and Risk Assessment (macro F1 **0.409 → 0.509**).

## Key Claims
- **Representational bottleneck.** A single SKILL.md entangles invocation interface, scene-level execution structure, and action/resource-use signals — forcing every downstream consumer to re-parse the long, noisy, sometimes incomplete prose.
- **Three layers grounded in classical theory.**
  - **Scheduling layer** (Memory Organization Packets, Schank 1980): goal, tags, intent signature, inputs/outputs — invocation-level signals.
  - **Structural layer** (Script Theory, Schank & Abelson 1977): ordered scenes (prepare / acquire / act / verify / finish / retry) with expectations and transitions.
  - **Logical layer** (Conceptual Dependency, Schank 1972): atomic actions (READ / CALL / WRITE / EXPORT / CHECK) tagged with the resources they touch (local files, credentials, external API).
- **Source-grounded, not source-replacing.** SSL is paired with the original SKILL.md, not a substitute; combined views (SKILL.md + SSL) win on Risk Assessment, suggesting SSL exposes complementary evidence.
- **Why Schank/Abelson over Minsky/Fillmore.** MOP / Script / CD distinguish goal-oriented contexts, ordered activities, and primitive operations — closer to the three kinds of evidence SSL disentangles than Minsky's frame slots or Fillmore's frame semantics.
- **Empirical results.** Skill Discovery: rich SSL-derived description view raises MRR@50 from 0.649 to 0.729 on 431 intent-level queries against 6,184 skills. Risk Assessment: combined SKILL.md + SSL view raises macro F1 from 0.409 to 0.509 across six risk dimensions on 252 labelled skills.
- **Open release.** SSL guidelines, normalizer prompts, 6,184-skill annotated corpus, 431 intent queries, and 252 risk-labelled skills released under COOLPKU/SSL.

## Key Quotes
> "Skills are still represented by text-heavy artifacts ... whose machine-usable evidence remains embedded largely in natural-language descriptions."
> "Semantically distinct properties are collapsed into a single textual surface."
> "SSL is hence designed to represent machine-facing skill artifacts."

## Connections
- [[pekinguniversity|PekingUniversity]] — institutional author.
- [[skillmd|SKILL.md]] — input format being structurally re-exposed.
- [[memoryorganizationpackets|MemoryOrganizationPackets]] — Schank's MOP basis for the scheduling layer.
- [[scripttheory|ScriptTheory]] — Schank & Abelson basis for the structural layer.
- [[conceptualdependency|ConceptualDependency]] — Schank basis for the logical layer.
- [[frametheory|FrameTheory]] — Minsky alternative considered.
- [[framesemantics|FrameSemantics]] — Fillmore alternative considered.
- [[skilldiscovery|SkillDiscovery]] — first evaluation task.
- [[riskassessment|RiskAssessment]] — second evaluation task.
- [[voyager|Voyager]] — predecessor skill-library system.
- [[2605.00424-skills-as-verifiable-artifacts|Metere]] — directly complementary: a structured skill representation makes the manifest's *capability declarations* machine-checkable, which is exactly the prerequisite for raising verification level above `unverified`.
- [[2605.02396-heavyskill]] — concerns the inner skill the LLM internalizes; SSL concerns the external skill artifact's machine-readable structure.

## Contradictions
- Argues against the prevailing pattern of more text + better embeddings as the path to better skill discovery; insists structural disentanglement is the missing primitive. Aligned with [[2605.00424-skills-as-verifiable-artifacts]] on treating skills as artifacts requiring formal-ish handling, but at the representation layer rather than the trust layer; the two papers compose: SSL exposes the facts that biconditional-style verification would need to check.

nodes.label: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
nodes.markdown:
---
title: "Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks"
type: source
tags: [paper, seq2seq, lstm, encoder-decoder, machine-translation, foundational]
date: 2014-09-10
sources: []
source_file: raw/1409.3215v3.pdf
last_updated: 2026-05-10
---

## Summary
Sutskever, Vinyals & Le (Google) introduce **sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) learning**: an end-to-end neural approach that maps variable-length input sequences to variable-length output sequences using two stacked LSTMs — one encoder that reads the input into a fixed-dimensional vector and one decoder that emits the output conditioned on that vector. On the WMT'14 English→French task, an ensemble of 5 deep LSTMs reaches BLEU 34.81 (vs. SMT baseline 33.30), the first time a pure neural translation system beats a phrase-based SMT baseline at scale. Using the LSTM to rescore the SMT 1000-best lifts BLEU to 36.5, within 0.5 of the prior best (37.0). Two surprising findings: the LSTM handles long sentences well, and **reversing the source-sentence word order** (but not the target) dropped perplexity from 5.8 → 4.7 and lifted BLEU 25.9 → 30.6 by introducing many short-term dependencies that ease optimization. This is the architectural predecessor of [[1706.03762-attention-is-all-you-need]] — same encoder-decoder framing, recurrent backbone replaced three years later by attention.

## Key Claims
- **Seq2seq framing.** A general sequence-mapping problem can be cast as `p(y₁,…,y_{T'} | x₁,…,x_T) = ∏ p(yt | v, y₁,…,y_{t-1})`, where `v` is the encoder LSTM's final hidden state. Decoder is essentially an LSTM language model conditioned on `v`.
- **Two separate LSTMs.** Using distinct encoder and decoder LSTMs (rather than tying weights) adds parameters at negligible cost and supports training on multiple language pairs jointly.
- **Depth matters.** 4-layer LSTMs significantly outperform shallow ones; each added layer reduces perplexity ~10%.
- **Source-reversal trick.** Mapping `c, b, a → α, β, γ` instead of `a, b, c → α, β, γ` shortens the "minimal time lag" between aligned source/target tokens, easing SGD. BLEU lifts from 25.9 → 30.6, perplexity drops 5.8 → 4.7. Effect extends to long sentences (better memory utilization).
- **Beam search decoding works at small B.** B=2 captures most of the benefit; B=1 already works.
- **LSTM rescoring of SMT n-best lists.** Averaging LSTM log-prob with SMT score on the 1000-best list lifts the SMT baseline from 33.30 → 36.5 BLEU.
- **Representation quality.** 2D PCA projection of the encoder's final hidden state shows that learned sentence embeddings are sensitive to word order yet relatively invariant to active/passive voice — early evidence that recurrent encoders learn meaning-bearing representations.
- **Long-sentence performance.** Contrary to the experience of [Cho et al. 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.1078) and [Bahdanau et al. 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473), reversed-source LSTMs degrade only marginally on long sentences — undermining the prior assumption that fixed-vector encoders cannot handle long inputs.

## Key Quotes
> "We present a general end-to-end approach to sequence learning that makes minimal assumptions on the sequence structure."

> "While we do not have a complete explanation to this phenomenon, we believe that it is caused by the introduction of many short term dependencies to the dataset. … By reversing the words in the source sentence, … the first few words in the source language are now very close to the first few words in the target language, so the problem's minimal time lag is greatly reduced."

> "It is the first time that a pure neural translation system outperforms a phrase-based SMT baseline on a large scale MT task by a sizeable margin, despite its inability to handle out-of-vocabulary words."

> "We conclude that it is important to find a problem encoding that has the greatest number of short term dependencies, as they make the learning problem much simpler."

## Architecture Reference (constants)
- 4-layer LSTM encoder + 4-layer LSTM decoder, 1000 cells per layer, 1000-dim word embeddings.
- Vocabulary: 160k source (English), 80k target (French); OOV → `UNK`. Sentence vector dimension: 8000.
- Parameters: 384M total, of which 64M are pure recurrent connections (32M encoder + 32M decoder).
- Training: WMT'14 EN→FR, 12M sentences (348M FR words, 304M EN words). Plain SGD, no momentum, LR 0.7 with halving every half-epoch after epoch 5, total 7.5 epochs. Uniform init [−0.08, 0.08]. Gradient norm clipped to 5 (per-128-batch). Length-bucketed minibatches (2× speedup).
- Hardware: 8 GPUs (one per LSTM layer + 4 for softmax parallelization), 6,300 words/sec, ~10 days training.
- Decoding: left-to-right beam search, B=12 for best results; B=2 captures most gains.

## Results (WMT'14 EN→FR, ntst14 test set, cased BLEU)

| System | BLEU |
|---|---|
| SMT baseline [Schwenk 2014] | 33.30 |
| Bahdanau et al. 2014 (attention) | 28.45 |
| Single forward LSTM (B=12) | 26.17 |
| Single reversed LSTM (B=12) | 30.59 |
| Ensemble of 5 reversed LSTMs (B=12) | **34.81** |
| Rescore SMT 1000-best w/ ensemble of 5 reversed LSTMs | **36.5** |
| Best WMT'14 result [Durrani et al. 2014] | 37.0 |
| Oracle rescoring of SMT 1000-best | ~45 |

## Connections
- [[SeqToSeq]] — the framework introduced here; encoder reads input to a fixed vector, decoder emits output token-by-token conditioned on it.
- [[EncoderDecoder]] — the high-level structural pattern; later inherited and re-instantiated with attention in [[1706.03762-attention-is-all-you-need]].
- [[LSTM]] — the recurrent unit used for both encoder and decoder.
- [[BeamSearch]] — the decoding procedure; B=2 already captures most of the gain.
- [[BLEU]] — the evaluation metric (cased multi-bleu.pl).
- [[MachineTranslation]] — the task; first large-scale win for a pure neural system.
- [[Google]] — author affiliation (Google Brain).
- [[Transformer]] — direct descendant: same encoder-decoder framing, recurrence replaced by self-attention.
- [[1706.03762-attention-is-all-you-need]] — the paper that supersedes the recurrent backbone with multi-head attention three years later; cites Bahdanau et al.'s attention work which itself was a response to the fixed-vector bottleneck of this paper.

## Contradictions
None with current wiki content. This source *predates* every other paper in the LLM corpus and supplies the encoder-decoder framing the Transformer paper inherits. The fixed-vector bottleneck that motivates the attention mechanism of Bahdanau et al. 2014 / [[1706.03762-attention-is-all-you-need]] is the central limitation of this paper's design — they are sequential refinements, not contradictions.

## Notes
- NeurIPS 2014 (NIPS 2014), Montréal. v3 of arXiv:1409.3215 (14 Dec 2014).
- Authors went on to define much of modern deep learning: Sutskever co-founded OpenAI; Vinyals leads DeepMind research; Le led Google Brain's AutoML work.
- The reversal trick is now mostly obsolete — attention-based architectures resolve the long-range-dependency problem structurally — but the empirical principle (*encode the problem to maximize short-term dependencies*) remains a recurring theme in training recipes.

## Summary
Sherwood, Aybar & Kaplan (U Chicago + independent) propose a benchmark for **recursive self-improvement (RSI)** early-warning signal: have frontier coding agents autonomously implement an AlphaZero-style Connect Four pipeline within a 3-hour, single-consumer-GPU budget given only a minimal task description. Trained agents play a round-robin tournament against the Pascal Pons solver. **Claude Opus 4.7** wins as first-mover against Pons in 7 of 8 trials — significantly beating other agents (≤2/8). The task was unsaturated when the study began in January 2026, near-saturated by submission, illustrating fast capability growth. A 16-trial probe surfaces anomalous **GPT-5.4** under-utilization of its time budget that is consistent with (but not diagnostic of) sandbagging.

## Key Claims
- **RSI early-warning** — replicating past AI breakthroughs likely falls before AI-accelerates-AI; complementing METR time horizon and ECI which measure broad capability growth.
- **Game-AI as objective metric** — external solvers (Pons) and game outcomes give scoring criteria independent of human grading.
- **Opus 4.7 dominates** — 7/8 wins as first-mover against Pons; statistically significantly above peers.
- **Anomalous GPT-5.4 behavior** — uses much less of its time budget than peers; shorter, less-evaluation-coded prompts increase usage but Bradley-Terry rating differences are only directional, not significant — consistent with sandbagging signature but not conclusive.
- **Cybersecurity context** — Claude Opus 4.6 reportedly scored 100% on Cybench; Anthropic withheld Claude Mythos partly over advanced cybersecurity capability (e.g. 27-year-old OpenBSD vulnerability discovery).

## Key Quotes
> "The task, which no frontier agent could reliably complete when we began development in January of 2026, is now near-saturation."
> "Past AI research breakthroughs likely could be replicated by AIs well in advance of a trendline break in capabilities indicating RSI."

## Summary
Builds \\(\mathbb{N}\\) from two angles: axiomatically via the Peano axioms (P1–P5 with successor function and induction), and concretely via von Neumann's set-theoretic construction \\(0 = \varnothing,\ S(n) = n \cup \{n\}\\). Defines addition and multiplication recursively, derives their algebraic properties, and discusses the well-ordering of \\(\mathbb{N}\\).

## Key Claims
- Peano axioms: \\(0 \in \mathbb{N}\\); successor stays in \\(\mathbb{N}\\); \\(0\\) is no successor; successor is injective; the induction axiom pins down \\(\mathbb{N}\\) as smallest model.
- Von Neumann construction: every \\(n\\) coincides with the set of its predecessors; \\(|n| = n\\).
- Addition/multiplication defined recursively from successor; both are associative, commutative; \\(0\\) is identity for \\(+\\), \\(1\\) for \\(\cdot\\); \\(\cdot\\) distributes over \\(+\\).
- \\(\mathbb{N}\\) has no zero divisors.
- Order \\(m \leq n \iff \exists k\, n = m+k\\) is a total well-ordering; well-ordering is equivalent to the induction principle.

## Key Quotes
> "Each natural number coincides with the set of all its predecessors, so that the number n has exactly n elements."
> "Well-ordering ... is logically equivalent to the principle of induction."

title: "Agentic World Modeling: Foundations, Capabilities, Laws, and Beyond"
type: source

## Summary
Chu, Zhang, Lin et al. (HKUST + NUS + Oxford + NTU + CUHK + HKU + UW + UTSD + SMU + HKUST-Guangzhou) survey **agentic world modeling** under a unifying **"levels × laws"** taxonomy. The capability axis distinguishes **L1 Predictor** (one-step local transition operators) → **L2 Simulator** (multi-step action-conditioned rollouts that respect domain laws) → **L3 Evolver** (autonomously revises its own model when predictions fail against new evidence). The law axis identifies four governing-law regimes — **physical, digital, social, scientific** — each constraining what a world model must satisfy and where it most likely fails. The paper synthesizes 400+ works and ~100 representative systems across model-based RL, video generation, web/GUI agents, multi-agent social simulation, and AI-driven scientific discovery, and proposes decision-centric evaluation principles plus a minimal reproducible evaluation package.

## Key Claims
- **Three capability levels** form a strict elevation hierarchy. L2 requires composing L1 transitions while respecting domain laws; L3 additionally requires online self-revision against new evidence.
- **Four law regimes** — physical, digital, social, scientific — drive different failure modes and require different inductive biases. Cross-domain analysis (§4.2.5) shows where techniques transfer and where they do not.
- **Prediction vs. decision-centric evaluation.** Prediction accuracy alone is insufficient; the paper proposes evaluating world models against the decisions they enable, with three boundary conditions and L1/L2/L3 differentiation criteria.
- **Architectural building blocks (§7).** State inference, forward dynamics, observation decoding, inverse dynamics — assembled differently across regimes (e.g. video generation vs. web agents vs. multi-agent social simulation).
- **Roadmap claim.** A path from passive next-step prediction toward world models that can simulate and ultimately reshape the environments in which agents operate; explicit "Beyond L3" speculation.
- **Connects previously isolated communities.** Model-based RL, video generative models, GUI/web agents, social simulation, and AI4Science were largely talking past each other; the levels × laws frame proposes a shared vocabulary.

## Key Quotes
> "World model carries different meanings across research communities."
> "L3 Evolver autonomously revises its own model when predictions fail against new evidence."
> "Charts a path from passive next-step prediction toward world models that can simulate, and ultimately reshape, the environments in which agents operate."

title: "HEAVYSKILL: Heavy Thinking as the Inner Skill in Agentic Harness"
type: source

## Summary
Wang et al. (Meituan LongCat Team + Peking U) argue that the apparent gains of orchestrated agentic harnesses come not from elaborate scaffolding but from an **inner skill** of "heavy thinking": **parallel reasoning** producing K trajectories, followed by **sequential deliberation** over a serialized memory cache. They show this two-stage workflow beats Best-of-N across STEM/coding/general benchmarks, that stronger LLMs approach Pass@N with it, and that depth+width of heavy thinking can be jointly improved with **RLVR** (reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards).

## Key Claims
- **Harness ≈ heavy thinking** — orchestration loops can be abstracted into parallel-reason-then-deliberate, internalized as one model skill.
- **Performance hierarchy** — Heavy-Pass@k ≥ Heavy-Mean@K ≥ Vote@K ≥ Mean@k on STEM benchmarks with verifiable answers.
- **Implicit verification in deliberation** — qualitative analysis: models compare trajectory differences during deliberation, acting as implicit verifiers.
- **Trajectory quality + diversity dominates** — ablations show parallel-stage trajectories' quality and diversity are the two main performance drivers; deliberation depends mostly on the deliberator's general capability, suggesting separate optimization may help.
- **RLVR scales heavy thinking** — depth (deliberation) and breadth (parallel generation) can be co-optimized to improve Heavy-Mean@k and Pass@k simultaneously.
- **Iterative deliberation** — re-feeding deliberation output back as cache enables progressive refinement, mirroring human iteration.

## Key Quotes
> "We abstract the agentic harness into the LLM's inherent capability of heavy thinking."
> "Models explicitly compare trajectory differences during deliberation, functioning as implicit verifiers."

title: "ODS Ch.2: Array-Based Lists"
type: source
tags: [book, data-structures, arrays, amortized-analysis]

author: "Pat Morin"
chapter: 2

## Summary
Implementations of the List and Queue interfaces backed by a single contiguous array. The fundamental tension: arrays give O(1) get/set but require shifting on add/remove and cannot resize without copy. The chapter resolves this with **amortized analysis** of doubling/halving — even though `resize()` is O(n), its total cost across m operations is O(m), giving O(1) amortized cost per operation. Covers ArrayStack (basic), ArrayQueue (modular indexing), ArrayDeque (front+back O(1)), DualArrayDeque (built from two stacks), and RootishArrayStack (space-efficient √n-block layout).

## Key Claims
- **ArrayStack**: get/set in O(1); add(i,x)/remove(i) in O(n−i) plus amortized O(1) for resize.
- **Resize policy**: grow when full (double the array); shrink when length(a) ≥ 3n (halve). The factor-3 hysteresis is what gives amortized O(1) — without it, alternating add/remove at the boundary forces O(n) resizes per op.
- **Amortization lemma (Lemma 2.1)**: any sequence of m add/remove on an empty ArrayStack incurs O(m) total resize cost. Proof: between successive resizes, n must change by at least n_i / 2.
- **ArrayQueue** uses modular arithmetic on a head pointer (j ← (j + 1) mod length(a)) so the queue can wrap around; resize when full.
- **ArrayDeque** generalizes to support front operations in O(min{i, n−i}) by choosing the cheaper end to shift toward.
- **DualArrayDeque** stacks two ArrayStacks back-to-back; rebalances when one is too small (factor-3 imbalance triggers a reshuffle).
- **RootishArrayStack** uses √n blocks of geometrically increasing sizes 1, 2, 3, ... → wastes only O(√n) space at any time vs O(n) for ArrayStack.

## Key Quotes
> "Although some individual operations are more expensive, the amortized cost, when amortized over all m operations, is only O(1) per operation."
> "If we ignore the cost of the potential call to resize(), then the cost of the add(i,x) operation is proportional to the number of elements we have to shift to make room for x."

## Connections
- [[ods-01-introduction]] — defines the List/Queue/Stack interfaces these implement.
- [[ods-03-linked-lists]] — pointer-based alternative with different cost trade-offs.
- [[ods-05-hash-tables]] — uses the same amortized doubling argument for ChainedHashTable resize.
- [[ods-10-heaps]] — BinaryHeap reuses the array-doubling strategy.
- [[matrices]] — backing arrays as 1-D analogue of matrix storage.

## Contradictions
None.

# Gemini

Family of natively multimodal foundation models from [[GoogleDeepMind]], introduced in [[2312.11805-gemini]] (December 2023). Built on [[Transformer]] decoders with [[MultiQueryAttention]]; trained jointly across text, image, audio, and video; deployed in three sizes:

| Variant | Role | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Ultra** | Frontier reasoning | First model to exceed human-expert [[MMLU]] (90.04%); SOTA on 30/32 benchmarks reported in 1.0. |
| **Pro** | Cost/latency-optimized | Powers default Gemini consumer chat and base of [[AlphaCode2]]. |
| **Nano-1 / Nano-2** | On-device | 1.8B / 3.25B params; 4-bit quantized; [[KnowledgeDistillation|distilled]] from larger Geminis. |

## Product variants

- **Gemini Apps** — consumer chat. Originally branded as **[[Bard]]** (powered by [[PaLM2]]); rebranded to *Gemini* (with Pro) and *Gemini Advanced* (with Ultra).
- **Gemini APIs** — developer-facing via Google AI Studio and Cloud Vertex AI.

Both variants share pre-training but diverge in post-training: instruction following, tool-use control loop (tools rendered as code blocks), multilinguality (40+ languages), multimodal vision SFT, and safety SFT/RLHF.

## Place in the wiki

Gemini is the second **substrate-defining** entry in the LLM corpus alongside [[1706.03762-attention-is-all-you-need]]. The 2017 paper defines the *architecture*; Gemini 1.0 defines the *frontier-multimodal-deployment template* — three-size family, native multimodality, [[RLHF]] flywheel, structured responsible-deployment review, [[DangerousCapabilities]] evaluation. Most 2026 agent papers in this wiki implicitly assume a Gemini-class base model when they discuss harnesses, memory, or skill verification.

# Google

Google's research arms — **Google Brain**, **Google Research**, and **Google AI Language** (now consolidated into **Google DeepMind**) — produced the three foundational sequence-modeling and pretraining papers in this wiki: [[1409.3215-seq2seq]] (Sutskever, Vinyals, Le — 2014), [[1706.03762-attention-is-all-you-need]] (Vaswani et al. — 2017), and [[1810.04805-bert]] (Devlin, Chang, Lee, Toutanova — 2018).

## Sequence-to-sequence learning (2014)

[[1409.3215-seq2seq]] introduces the encoder-decoder framing that powers all subsequent neural MT and language modeling. Authors:
- Ilya Sutskever — later co-founded [[OpenAI]].
- Oriol Vinyals — now leads research at Google DeepMind.
- Quoc V. Le — led Google Brain's AutoML and continued sequence-modeling work.

## Attention Is All You Need (2017)

Authors of that paper, all affiliated with Google at submission (with one exception):
- Ashish Vaswani (Google Brain)
- Noam Shazeer (Google Brain)
- Niki Parmar (Google Research)
- Jakob Uszkoreit (Google Research)
- Llion Jones (Google Research)
- Aidan N. Gomez (University of Toronto; work performed while at Google Brain)
- Łukasz Kaiser (Google Brain)
- Illia Polosukhin (work performed while at Google Research)

The paper's tensor2tensor codebase was open-sourced at https://github.com/tensorflow/tensor2tensor.

## BERT (2018)

[[1810.04805-bert]] introduces [[BERT]] — a deep bidirectional Transformer encoder pre-trained with [[MaskedLanguageModel]] + [[NextSentencePrediction]] objectives — and the pretrain-then-finetune transfer-learning recipe that dominates NLP from 2018 onward. Google AI Language authors:
- Jacob Devlin
- Ming-Wei Chang
- Kenton Lee
- Kristina Toutanova

Code and pre-trained checkpoints at https://github.com/google-research/bert.

## Role in the wiki

Google is the architectural origin of every modern large language model in this wiki. The 2014 [[SeqToSeq]] paper established the encoder-decoder framing; the 2017 [[Transformer]] paper replaced its recurrent backbone with self-attention; the 2018 [[BERT]] paper supplied the pretrain-then-finetune transfer-learning recipe. Every subsequent LLM in the AI/LLM corpus inherits this substrate.
